Let $\text{M}$ be a finite automaton and let $\text{M}^{\prime}$ be obtained from $\text{M}$ by interchanging the collections of accepting and non-accepting states. i.e. If $\text{Q}$ is the set of states in $\text{M}$ and $\text{F}$ is the set of accepting states in $\text{M}$ then $\text{Q} \backslash \text{F}$ is the set of accepting states in $\text{M}’.$
Now consider the following statements :

  1. If $\text{M}$ is deterministic, then the language accepted by $\text{M}^{\prime}$ is the complement of the language accepted by $\text{M} .$
  2. If $\text{M}$ is Non-deterministic, then the language accepted by $\text{M}^{\prime}$ is the complement of the language accepted by $\text{M} .$

Which of the above is/are correct?

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.text: Let $\mathrm{M}=(\mathrm{Q}, \Sigma, \delta, q0, \mathrm{~F})$ be a DFA. If $\mathrm{F}$ contains at least one state, the language of $\text{M}$ must be nonempty.

Let $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ be regular languages. Let $\text{A-B}$ consist of all the strings in $\text{A}$ which are not in $\text{B}$ (this is sometimes written $\text{A} \backslash \text{B}$ and is also called the set difference). Then $\text{A-B}$ is regular.
Let $\text{M}=(\mathrm{Q}, \Sigma, \delta, q0, \text{F})$ be a DFA. If $F$ is empty (i.e. No final state), the language of $\text{M}$ must be empty.
Let $\mathrm{M}=(\mathrm{Q}, \Sigma, \delta,q0, \mathrm{~F})$ be a DFA. If $\mathrm{F}$ contains $q0,$ the language of $\mathrm{M}$ must be nonempty.

questions.solution:
Answer: B, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 30)
Option A ). It is False because having a final state in DFA does not guarantee that language must be non-empty. Because if that final state is unreachable from the initial state, the language is empty.

But instead of DFA if it is minimal DFA then this option must be true. Because in Minimal DFA unreachable states are not allowed. Language must be nonempty if the final state is there in minimal DFA.

Option B). It is TRUE, As A and B are regular already given, then using Product Construction we can have A – B DFA also so if we have DFA then the language must be regular.

Option C). It is trivially true. No final state means the language is empty.

Option D). It is also true. Because the initial state is a final state there are two reasons of the language cannot be non-empty.

1). Since the initial is final then the final is reachable from the initial.

2). An empty string must belong to the language iff the initial state is a final state in the case of DFA. so the language is non-empty.

The answer is B, C, D.
Source solution 2 (score: 16)

If all final states are unreachable then $\text{L}$ is empty. If $\text{F}$ contains $q0,$ the language of $\text{M}$ must be nonempty because at least empty string will be in $\text{L}.$

Source solution 1 (score: 72)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/1MiJGnZluLs

The DFA shown above describes a language over $\{0,1\}$ that contains strings with exactly $2\; 0's.$

For length $10,$ we have a total $2^{(10)}=1024$ strings, out of which $10 \mathrm{C} 2= 45$ strings have exactly $2$ zeros. Hence, the answer is $1024-45=979$.

Note that Because the language $L$ is defined by a DFA $M,$ it is a regular language. A regular language is always a context free language. That is because a CFL is defined by a PDA and a PDA is equivalent to a NFA with a stack-so it includes all NFA's.

The following statement is known as "the pumping lemma for regular language":

If $\mathrm{A}$ is a regular language, then there is a number $p$ (the pumping length) where, if $s$ is any string in $\text{A}$ of length at least $p$, then $s$ can be divided into $3$ pieces, $s = xyz$, satisfying the following conditions:

  1. For each $i \geq 0, x y^{i} z \in \text{A},$
  2. $|y|>0$, and
  3. $|x y| \leq p$

Your friend John is trying to prove that the language $w w^{R}$, the language of even length palindromes over $\{0,1\}$, is not regular.
For pumping length $p$ he chooses the string $\mathrm{S}$. Which of the following strings, can he use for the pumping lemma for regular languages to prove that this language is not regular?
questions.solution:

following:
$$

$$
When we pump it, we get something of the form $01^{i} 0$, where $i\geq 2 p -2$ and $i$ is even. This is always a even length palindrome.
Note that if you choose $1^{p} 01^{p}$ then you cannot pump it.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following statements :

  1. If a deterministic finite automaton $\text{M}$ accepts at least one string, then it accepts at least one string whose length is less than the number of states in $\text{M}.$
  2. If a non-deterministic finite automaton $\text{M}$ accepts at least one string, then it accepts at least one string whose length is less than the number of states in $\text{M}.$

Which of the above statements is/are true?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 33)
Assume that a FA(DFA or NFA) accepts a string w of length greater than or equal to $n,$ where $n$ is the number of states in that FA, then to process the first $n$ symbols of this string, the FA has to go through a sequence of at least $n+1$ states but there are only $n$ distinct states so by pigeon hole principle, some state must repeat. So, we can remove that repetition and get a smaller string which belongs to our language. Hence, we would have a string in the language which has length less than the number of states in FA. So both statements are true.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)
Statement 1 (DFA)

Suppose a DFA has 5 states.

The statement says:

If the DFA accepts any string, then it must accept at least one string of length less than 5.

Why?

Take the shortest accepted string.

While reading this string, imagine the DFA moves through states.

  • If it visits the same state twice, then it has gone in a loop.
  • That loop is unnecessary because you can remove it and still reach the accepting state.
  • This would give an even shorter accepted string, which is impossible since we already chose the shortest one.

So, in the shortest accepted string:

  • No state is repeated.
  • Therefore, the DFA can visit at most all 5 states once.
  • Visiting 5 states means only 4 transitions (edges), so the string length is at most 4, which is less than 5.

Hence, Statement 1 is True.

Statement 2 (NFA)

Now consider an NFA with 5 states.

The idea is exactly the same.

Choose the shortest accepted string.

  • If an accepting path repeats a state, then there is a loop.
  • Remove that loop.
  • The NFA will still reach the accepting state.
  • Now you have a shorter accepted string, which is a contradiction.

So, in the shortest accepting path:

  • No state repeats.
  • Therefore, it uses at most 5 states and 4 transitions.
  • So the accepted string has length less than 5.

Hence, Statement 2 is also True.

Easy Trick to Remember (for exams)

Shortest accepted string ⇒ No repeated state.

Why?

Because repeating a state means there is a loop, and removing the loop makes the string shorter.

Therefore:

  • DFA with n states → shortest accepted string has length < n.
  • NFA with n states → shortest accepted string also has length < n.

Final Answer: C. Both

A DFA accepts infinitely many strings iff there exists a loop in the path from initial state to any final state.

The language is given to be finite. Therefore, the DFA must contain at least one sink (dead) state.

Since the DFA has \(100\) states, out of which \(1\) is a sink state, a string of length at most \(98\) can be accepted.

We know that for a finite language, the minimum pumping length is
\[
p_{\min} = |\text{longest string}| + 1.
\]

Now, for \(w \in L\),
\[
0 \leq |w| \leq 98.
\]

Therefore, it is possible that the maximum length of a string in \(L\) is only \(49\). Hence,
\[
p_{\min} = 49 + 1 = 50.
\]

questions.qtext: Let $\mathrm{D}$ be some DFA (Deterministic Finite Automata) with $10$ states and let the cardinality of the input alphabet set be $3.$ If the language accepted by $\mathrm{D}$ i.e., $\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{D})$ is finite, the maximum value of $|\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{D})|$ will be _______, $(|\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{D})|$ denotes the cardinality of $\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{D}))$
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 57)

Answer $: 9841$

$\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis:}}$ https://youtu.be/kPLciwgwKaE

Since the language is Finite, We cannot have loops in the way from the initial state to the final state.

And Since we need to maximize the cardinality of $L(D)$, so, we need as many final states as possible while preserving the finiteness of the $L(D)$.
So, the DFA will look like this :



Where all the states except the last one are final states, and the last state is a non-final trap state.

The last state $q_L$ is a trap state (i.e. $\delta(q_L, a) = q_L, \forall a \in \Sigma$ ) and non-final as well.

So, $\operatorname{\max}(|L(D)|)=\Sigma^{0}+\Sigma^{1}+\Sigma^{2} \ldots \ldots+\Sigma^{n-2}$

Hence, the answer is $9841.$

Why is the last state a trap state??

Because if it is not a trap state, then you need to make a transition from last state to some other state & if you do so, then a loop will occur which makes language infinite.

NOTE: The following Video Solution covers the Variation in case of NFA as well.

$\color{red}{\text{Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis:}}$ https://youtu.be/kPLciwgwKaE

Source solution 2 (score: 24)

This way I approach the question , I hope it will help you .


Thank You !

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Answer: 9841

Explanation:

  • Preventing Cycles: For the DFA to accept a finite language, it cannot have cycles. It must transition linearly and end in a single "dead state" (trap state) that loops on itself.

  • Available States: Out of the 10 states, 1 is the dead state, leaving 9 sequential states ($q_0$ to $q_8$).

  • Maximizing Paths: To maximize combinations, make all 9 sequential states accepting states. Use all 3 input symbols to transition from state $q_i$ directly to $q_{i+1}$.

  • Geometric Growth: The number of unique strings accepted at each state grows by powers of the alphabet size ($3$):

    • Strings at $q_0$: $3^0$

    • Strings at $q_1$: $3^1$

    • ...

    • Strings at $q_8$: $3^8$

  • Calculation: The total maximum cardinality is the sum of this geometric progression:

    $$|L(D)| = 3^0 + 3^1 + 3^2 + \dots + 3^8$$

    $$|L(D)| = \frac{3^9 - 1}{3 - 1} = \frac{19683 - 1}{2} = 9841$$
